messages.subject: format of data table for lrm
messages.subject_clean: format of data table for lrm
messages.body_plain:
Hi everybody,

in the context of an empirical study about stress
placement with Italian learners of German as a
FL, Stefan Gries’s book „Statistik für
Sprachwissenschaftler“ (Ch. 4.1.2.2) has already
turned out to be very useful to me in comparing
frequencies of right/wrong answers with Chi-square-tests.

Having more than one independent variable, I
wondered if I could use a regression analysis,
too. The dependent variable would be nominal
(dichotomous), i.e. the right/wrong stress
placement, the independent variables would be
nominal or categorical. I guess, the right
analysis for this case is the binary logistic regression (Ch. 5.4).

My problem is the format of the data (table).

It seems to me, that the lrm-function needs a
table in which each production (=each word read
by a learner) has a row on its own, something like this:

WORD           ANSWER      PENULT        INTERF
Elefant           right                yes                   no
Elefant           wrong             yes                  no
Elefant           right                yes                  no
...
Symptom        right                yes                  yes
Symptom        wrong             yes                  yes
...

The first column (WORD) is only for illustration,
ANSWER is the dependent variable, PENULT (i.e.
stress on the penult in the plural form) and
INTERF (i.e. interference with L1 Italian) are the independent variables.

My Excel-data, however, are already aggregated,
with one row for each word (read by, let’s say
n=8 learners), thus the table is similar to the
following (where R_ANSWERS is the number of right answers):

WORD           R_ANSWERS           PENULT        INTERF
Elefant            6                                 yes                  no
Symptom        7                                 yes                  yes
Cholera           1                                 no                    yes
...

Transforming this table manually (with copy &
paste) in the one above would be quite
time-consuming because the words are about 150
and the real n=26. So my questions are:

1. Is there any way to make lrm accept my frequency data?
2. Or (otherwise): is there any rapid way of table transforming with R?

Thanks for your help,
Peter Paschke

messages.subject_clean: [StatForLing with R] format of data table for lrm
messages.body_plain:
Re question 1: yes, there is: you make the dependent variable a matrix
with two columns (using cbind).

Re question 2: yes, there is:
# example data
WORD <- c("Elefant","Symptom","Cholera")
R_ANSWERS <- c(6,7,1)
PENULT <- c("yes","yes","no")
INTERF <- c("no","yes","yes")
DAT <- data.frame(WORD, R_ANSWERS, PENULT, INTERF)

# conversion code from Michael J. Crawley (2007:189)
DAT.2 <- as.data.frame(lapply(DAT[,c(1,3,4)], function (x) rep(x, DAT[,2])))

Cheers,
STG
--
Stefan Th. Gries
-----------------------------------------------
University of California, Santa Barbara
http://www.linguistics.ucsb.edu/faculty/stgries

messages.subject: How can I change the reference values in logistic regression?
messages.subject_clean: How can I change the reference values in logistic regression?
messages.body_plain:
Hello everybody,

I'm using the logistic regression model (lrm) from the design package (described in Ch. 5.4 of Stefan Gries's book) with binary independent variables like PENULT (=PU or NPU), FREQUENCY (=High or Low) and so on.

My question is: How I can change the reference values of each of these variables in lrm (i.e. the values that don't appear in the model output)?
In other words, in:

PENULT=PU                  2.1719 0.14288 15.20  0.0000
INTERF=NIF                 2.3856 0.13351 17.87  0.0000
SCHWA=NoHelp              -1.2486 0.12608 -9.90  0.0000
LEXNEIGH=NoFriend         -0.8557 0.08665 -9.88  0.0000
FREQUENCY=Low             -0.3451 0.12818 -2.69  0.0071
PENULT=PU * INTERF=NIF    -1.3266 0.18529 -7.16  0.0000
PENULT=PU * FREQUENCY=Low -0.5712 0.17234 -3.31  0.0009

Thanks for your help,

Peter

Hi, a very simple way to do it is to rename your values putting
figures before each value:

1PU, 2NPU => now PU will be automatically chosen as the reference
value
1NIF, 2IF

Maybe this helps too.

Clara

messages.subject: interactions in lrm output
messages.body_plain:
Hello everyone,

below you can see some lrm output with factors (and some significant interactions) that seem to influence the correct stress placement in German loan words which have cognates in the L1 of Italian learners. Initially I wondered why the factors PENULT=PU and INTERF=NIF had a positive effect on right answers (right stress placement), while their interaction PENULT=PU * INTERF=NIF did not. Obviously, my interpretation of interaction was wrong. Looking in Stefan's chapter about logistic regression, I did not find explanations, but a similar case: V_CHANGPOSS=no and PAT_ACT both have positive values, but their interaction has a negative coefficient and an effect size smaller than one: 0.76.

I looked for some explanation elsewhere, and now I think it might be like this: The effect size value of 0.76 compares two odds ratios: a) the odds ratio of construction=1 (with "to") in sentences with V_CHANGPOSS=no and PAT_ACT=x+1 (compared to PAT_ACT=x); b) the odds ratio of construction=1  in sentences with V_CHANGPOSS=yes and PAT_ACT=x+1 (compared to PAT_ACT=x). So, the effect size of the interaction compares the effect of PAT_ACT in sentences with no possession change with the effect of PAT_ACT in sentences with possession change: the first one is weaker, it is 76% of the second one. Is this true?

In my case, it would mean that for words with PENULT=PU (i.e. stress on the penult) the (positive) influence of  INTERF=NIF (i.e. no risk of L1 interference) is much weaker than for words with PENULT=NPU (the reference level). This interpretation would make sense for my explanation of stress placement. But is it right?

Greetings from Italy,
Peter Paschke

messages.body_plain:
Not knowing what the levels of the dependent variable are etc., what
happens is that

- PENULT=PU on its own raises the probability of the predicted level
of the dependent variable, and
- INTERF=NIF on its own raises the probability of the predicted level
of the dependent variable even more, but
- PENULT=PU and INTERF=NIF *together* lower the probability of the
predicted level of the dependent variable.

Prose like this is why I myself pay less and less attention to
coefficients (with 3- and 4-way interactions it becomes even more of a
mess). Graphs are simply more meaningful, and this should give you a
better idea of what happens:

barplot(tapply(fitted(modell.lrm), list(PENULT, INTERF), mean),
beside=TRUE, legend=TRUE)

Just FYI: the paper at
(<http://www.linguistics.ucsb.edu/faculty/stgries/research/XXX_STG-SW_RegrTransl_XXX.pdf>)
explains all of this better and if ever a second revised edition of
the stats book were desired, that's how I would write this now.

HTH,
STG
--
Stefan Th. Gries

messages.body_plain:
Thank you very much, Stefan.
The paper was quite helpful for me. Now I understand that for interactions the probability is based on the sum of coefficients.

Using the same example as before:

>                            Coef    S.E.    Wald Z P
> Intercept                  -1.6423 0.10027 -16.38 0.0000
> PENULT=PU                   1.6008 0.12865  12.44 0.0000
> INTERF=NIF                  2.3856 0.13351  17.87 0.0000
> SCHWA=Help                  1.2486 0.12608   9.90 0.0000
> LEXNEIGH=Friend             0.8557 0.08665   9.88 0.0000
> FREQUENCY=High              0.3451 0.12818   2.69 0.0071
> PENULT=PU * INTERF=NIF     -1.3266 0.18529  -7.16 0.0000
> PENULT=PU * FREQUENCY=High  0.5712 0.17234   3.31 0.0009

..., to calculate the probability of right stress placement (the dependent binary variable) for words with the (binary) variables PENULT=PU and INTERF=NIF,
we have to sum the coeff. of Intercept, Interf=NIF and PENULT=PU * INTERF=NIF:
= -1.6423 + 2.3856 -1.3266 = -0.5833
The probability then is P = 1/(1+exp(--0.5833)= 38,5%, Right?
But this value is true only if all other independet variables have their reference levels, isn't it?

On the other hand (tapply did'nt work with the lrm model, so I used glm):
tapply(fitted(modell.glm), list(PENULT, INTERF), mean
           IF      NIF
NPU 0.2456897 0.828614
PU  0.7644979 0.896311
seems to calculate the mean of the probabilities of all words that fulfil certain conditions regardless of the values of the other independent variables. Otherwise it would be strange that the mean probability of right answers for PU-NIF-words is much higher here, almost 90%.

Peter Paschke, Italy
